scenes.heading: Fuels: fossil and renewable
scenes.sub: Where our energy comes from, and what it costs
scenes.say: Electricity, petrol cars and gas cooktops all depend on fuels, and most are still fossil fuels. But fossil fuels release carbon dioxide and will run out. So what are the alternatives?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A tap fed by rain keeps refilling; a tank filled long ago runs dry
scenes.science: Renewable fuels are replaced as fast as we use them
scenes.breaks: renewable fuels still need land, water, sunlight and time to grow the biomass, so supply isn't unlimited.
scenes.say: A renewable fuel is like a tap fed by rain: it's replaced as fast as you use it. A fossil fuel is like a tank filled long ago, refilling by a drop a year while you drain it with a hose. The key is the rate of replacement.

scenes.heading: Fossil fuels
points: Coal, crude oil, natural gas (mostly CH₄)
Formed over millions of years
Energy-dense and easy to store
Release long-stored carbon as CO₂
Also SO₂, nitrogen oxides, CO and soot
scenes.say: Coal, crude oil and natural gas formed from ancient organisms over millions of years. They're energy-dense and easy to store, but burning them releases carbon that was locked away underground, plus pollutants like sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.

scenes.heading: Renewable options
points: Biogas: anaerobic digestion of waste
Bioethanol: fermentation of glucose
Biodiesel: transesterification of oils
Green hydrogen: electrolysis, renewable power
Food vs fuel: crops compete for land
scenes.say: Biogas, mostly methane, comes from bacteria breaking down waste without oxygen. Bioethanol comes from fermenting crop sugars with yeast. Biodiesel is made from vegetable oils or fats. Hydrogen is renewable only when made using renewable electricity. And growing fuel crops can compete with food.

scenes.heading: Fermentation
parts: does the job, with no oxygen
scenes.say: In fermentation, yeast splits one glucose into two ethanol and two carbon dioxide, with no oxygen. Check the carbons: six on each side.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: What mass of ethanol can be made by fermenting 1.00 kg of glucose?
scenes.say: One kilogram of glucose is five point five five six moles. Each glucose gives two ethanol, so that's eleven point one one moles. Multiply by forty-six: five hundred and eleven grams of ethanol.
scenes.caption: 1.00 kg of glucose is 5.556 mol. Each glucose gives two ethanol, so that's 11.11 mol. Multiply by 46.0: 511 g of ethanol.

scenes.heading: Old carbon vs new carbon

left.title: Fossil fuels
points: Carbon locked away for millions of years
Burning adds extra CO₂ to the air
Adds to the enhanced greenhouse effect

right.title: Biofuels
points: Carbon taken from the air recently
Burning returns that CO₂
Not perfectly neutral: farming uses fuel

scenes.say: Both release carbon dioxide when burned. The difference is where the carbon came from. Fossil fuels unlock carbon buried for millions of years. Biofuels return carbon that plants absorbed recently. But farming and transport use fossil fuels, so biofuels are nearly carbon neutral, never perfectly.

points: Renewable depends on the rate of replacement
Fossil fuels release long-stored carbon
Biogas, bioethanol, biodiesel come from biomass
Biofuels: lower net CO₂, not zero
Hydrogen is only as green as its electricity
scenes.say: Quick recap. Renewable is about the rate of replacement. Fossil fuels release old carbon. Biofuels come from biomass and have lower net emissions, but they aren't perfectly carbon neutral. Now try the practice questions!
